questions.q: On a cold evening, a heater stands on the floor of a closed room. After half an hour, where in the room is the warmest air most likely to be found, and why?
questions.a: Near the ceiling, as warm air is less dense and moves up
o: Near the ceiling, as warm air is less dense and moves up
Near the floor, as warm air is heavier and stays down
Spread evenly, as heating does not change the air's density
Near the floor, as heating adds mass to the air around it

questions.q:
A solid metal ball has a mass of 79 g and a volume of 10.0 cm³ at room temperature. After heating, its volume is 10.1 cm³.
(a) Find its density before and after heating.
(b) Using (a), state which of mass, volume and density did not change, and explain why the density fell.
questions.a: (a) Before: 79 ÷ 10.0 = 7.9 g/cm³; after: 79 ÷ 10.1 = about 7.82 g/cm³. (b) The mass (79 g) did not change. Heating made the particles move apart, so the volume increased; the same mass in a larger volume gives a lower density.
s: (a) 7.9 and about 7.82 g/cm³
(b) mass unchanged; volume up, so density down

questions.q:
Consider these statements about what changes the density of a substance.
Statement 1: When a solid is heated, its mass increases, so its density increases.
Statement 2: Pressure has only a small effect on the density of a liquid.
Statement 3: Pressing on a solid changes its density more than pressing on a liquid does.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
At a mela in Jaipur, a tethered hot air balloon has an envelope holding 2000 m³ of air. The balloon fabric, basket, burner and riders together have a mass of 300 kg. The operator's sheet gives the density of air (illustrative values): 1.25 kg/m³ at 10 °C, 1.16 kg/m³ at 30 °C, 1.06 kg/m³ at 60 °C and 0.97 kg/m³ at 90 °C. The sheet's rule: the balloon rises only if the mass of the hot air inside plus 300 kg is less than the mass of 2000 m³ of the outside air.
(a) Explain why heating the air inside the envelope lowers its density.
(b) On a 30 °C afternoon, will the balloon rise if the air inside is heated to 60 °C? Show the masses.
(c) On a 10 °C morning, will it rise with the air inside at 60 °C? Show the masses.
(d) The operator says, 'We fly in the cool mornings because we need less heating.' Use (b) and (c), and the 90 °C value, to judge his statement.
questions.a: (a) On heating, the air particles move apart and the air spreads out, so its volume increases while its mass stays the same; density = mass ÷ volume falls, so 2000 m³ of hot air has less mass than 2000 m³ of cooler air. (b) Outside: 2000 × 1.16 = 2320 kg. Inside: 2000 × 1.06 = 2120 kg + 300 kg = 2420 kg. 2420 is more than 2320, so it will not rise. (c) Outside: 2000 × 1.25 = 2500 kg. Inside: 2120 + 300 = 2420 kg, less than 2500 kg, so it rises. (d) He is right. In the afternoon even 60 °C is not enough; the air must be heated to about 90 °C (2000 × 0.97 = 1940 + 300 = 2240 kg, less than 2320 kg). In the cold morning 60 °C is already enough, because the cold outside air is denser, so less heating is needed.
s: (a) heating increases volume at the same mass, so density falls
(b) 2420 kg vs 2320 kg: does not rise
(c) 2420 kg vs 2500 kg: rises
(d) agrees, using 60 °C enough in the morning but about 90 °C needed in the afternoon (2240 vs 2320 kg)

questions.q: A student reports: 'I heated 100 g of water from 20 °C to 60 °C. Its volume stayed at 100 mL the whole time, and its density rose from 1.00 g/mL to 1.02 g/mL.' Show that the report contradicts itself, and say what is likely to have really happened to the volume and the density.
questions.a: If the mass stayed 100 g and the volume stayed 100 mL, density = 100 ÷ 100 = 1.00 g/mL; it could not become 1.02 g/mL without the mass increasing or the volume decreasing, and neither happened in a simple heating. So the report contradicts itself. In fact, on heating, the particles spread out, so the volume of the water increases slightly while the mass stays the same, and the density decreases a little (below 1.00 g/mL).
s: same mass and volume must give the same density (1.00 g/mL)
so a rise to 1.02 g/mL is impossible as reported
what really happens: volume rises slightly, density falls

questions.q: A sealed balloon of air, a sealed plastic bottle completely full of water and a steel ball are each squeezed with the same large force. Which order gives the change in density from largest to smallest?
questions.a: Air, then water, then steel
o: Air, then water, then steel
Steel, then water, then air
Water, then air, then steel
All change equally, as the force is the same

questions.q: 200 g of cooking oil occupies 230 cm³ when heated to 80 °C. Rounded to two decimal places, its density at 80 °C is ___ g/cm³.
True or false? 'Water at 4 °C is denser than water at 0 °C, even though 0 °C is colder.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Generally cooling increases density, but water is special: its density is highest at 4 °C. Below 4 °C, as it approaches freezing at 0 °C, it expands, so water at 0 °C is less dense than water at 4 °C.
s: verdict: true
reason: water's density is highest at 4 °C; below that it expands as it nears freezing

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Squeezing a steel bolt hard in a vice hardly changes its density.
Reason (R): The particles in a solid are already very close to each other.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A wholesale shop sells cooking oil by the litre. The oil's density is 0.92 g/mL at 15 °C (early morning) and 0.90 g/mL at 40 °C (a May afternoon) (illustrative values).
(a) Which contains more oil by mass: 1 L measured in the morning or 1 L measured in the afternoon? Explain why.
(b) Find the mass of 100 L of oil measured at each temperature.
(c) A hotel pays the same price per litre at any time of day. When should it buy, and how much more oil (in kg) does it get per 100 L?
(d) The shopkeeper says, 'Oil gains weight in winter.' Correct his statement.
(e) Find the relative density of the oil at 15 °C, taking the density of water at 15 °C as 1.00 g/mL.
questions.a: (a) The morning litre: at the lower temperature the oil is denser, so each litre holds more mass; on heating the same mass spreads into a larger volume. (b) 100 L = 100 000 mL: at 15 °C, 0.92 × 100 000 = 92 000 g = 92 kg; at 40 °C, 0.90 × 100 000 = 90 000 g = 90 kg. (c) In the cool morning; it gets 92 − 90 = 2 kg more per 100 L. (d) The mass of the oil does not change with temperature. In cold weather its volume becomes smaller, so its density increases and a litre holds more oil; it does not gain mass. (e) 0.92 ÷ 1.00 = 0.92 (no unit).
s: (a) the morning litre, because the oil is denser when cooler
(b) 92 kg and 90 kg
(c) buy in the morning; 2 kg more per 100 L
(d) mass is unchanged; the volume shrinks so density rises
(e) 0.92, no unit

questions.q:
A glass of water at 25 °C is put in a refrigerator until it reaches 10 °C, and is then moved to a freezer, where it turns into ice at 0 °C.
(a) What happens to its density as it cools from 25 °C to 10 °C? Why?
(b) What happens to its density when it freezes into ice? Why?
questions.a: (a) It increases: on cooling the particles come closer, so the volume decreases while the mass stays the same. (b) It decreases: as water turns into ice its particles arrange themselves in a way that takes up more space (expansion), so the same mass occupies a larger volume.
s: (a) density rises on cooling: smaller volume, same mass
(b) density falls on freezing: water expands into ice

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the explanation in Column II.
Column I
1. Air above a candle flame moves upward
2. An ice cube floats in a glass of water
3. A cycle tyre holds much more air after pumping, though its size hardly changes
4. A brick under a heavy load keeps practically the same density
Column II
a. Particles of solids are already very close to each other
b. Heating increases volume while mass stays the same
c. Water takes up more space when it freezes
d. Pressure pushes gas particles closer together

A fixed amount of air, kept at the same temperature throughout, ends up with exactly twice its starting density.
(i) What must have happened to its volume? Explain.
(ii) Describe a simple situation that would produce this result.
(iii) Would squeezing the same volume of water in the same way give a similar result? Explain.
questions.a: (i) Its volume must have halved: density = mass ÷ volume, the mass is fixed and the temperature did not change, so twice the density needs half the volume. (ii) For example, the nozzle of a syringe holding 40 mL of air is sealed and the plunger is pushed in until the air occupies 20 mL; the pressure pushes the gas particles closer together. (iii) No. Liquids are nearly incompressible, so pressure has only a small effect on the density of water; it could not be squeezed to half its volume.
s: (i) volume halved, as mass is fixed
(ii) a situation where pressure squeezes a gas to half its volume
(iii) no: water is nearly incompressible

questions.q: A fixed amount of air is held in a container. Which change will increase the density of this air the most?
questions.a: Cooling it and squeezing it into a smaller space
o: Cooling it and squeezing it into a smaller space
Heating it and letting it spread into a bigger space
Heating it while it is sealed in a rigid metal box
Letting it spread into a bigger box at the same temperature

questions.q:
In a very cold winter, the surface of a lake in Ladakh freezes, and fish survive in the water below.
(a) Explain why the ice ends up as a layer on top of the lake.
(b) Predict what would happen to the lake and its fish in winter if ice were denser than liquid water. Give your reasoning.
questions.a: (a) Water expands as it freezes, so the same mass of ice takes up a larger volume and is less dense than liquid water; the ice therefore floats. (b) The ice would sink as it formed, so no floating layer would cover the lake; ice could pile up from the bottom and the lake could freeze through, leaving no water kept warm enough below for the fish to survive.
s: (a) ice is less dense because water expands on freezing, so it floats
(b) ice would sink, no protective top layer, the lake could freeze through and the fish would not survive

questions.q: Dev says: 'Heating makes air lighter because it loses some of its mass, and that is why hot air rises.' Do you agree? Explain what really happens.
questions.a: No. Heating does not change the mass of the air. When air is heated its particles move apart and spread out, so its volume increases while its mass stays the same. Its density (mass ÷ volume) therefore decreases, and the hot air rises because it is less dense than the cooler air around it, which is how a hot air balloon works.
s: verdict: disagree; mass does not change
heating increases volume, so density decreases
hot air rises because it is less dense than the surrounding cooler air

questions.q:
Rafiq checks his cycle tube before a trip to Lonavala. The tube holds 2 L of air when inflated, and its volume hardly changes when more air is pumped in. Before pumping, the air in it has a density of 1.2 g/L. After pumping, the air inside has a density of 3.6 g/L (illustrative values; temperature unchanged).
(a) Find the mass of air in the tube before pumping.
(b) Working backwards from the density after pumping, find how many grams of air the pump pushed in.
(c) Explain, using particles, how the same 2 L space can hold three times as much air.
(d) The tube maker says the air inside must stay between 3.0 g/L and 4.2 g/L, and on a smooth road a firmer tube (more air packed in) rolls more easily. Rafiq's ride is all on smooth road. Should he pump to 3.6 g/L, 4.2 g/L or 4.8 g/L? Find the mass of air the tube would then hold.
questions.a: (a) 2 L × 1.2 g/L = 2.4 g. (b) After: 2 L × 3.6 g/L = 7.2 g, so 7.2 − 2.4 = 4.8 g of air was pushed in. (c) Increasing the pressure pushes the gas particles closer together; there is a lot of space between gas particles, so more particles fit into the same volume and the density rises. (d) 4.2 g/L: it packs in the most air that the maker allows, so the tube is as firm as permitted for the smooth road; 4.8 g/L is above the maker's limit, and 3.6 g/L is softer than needed. Mass = 2 L × 4.2 g/L = 8.4 g (6.0 g more than before pumping).
s: (b) 4.8 g pushed in (7.2 g after)
(c) pressure pushes gas particles closer, so more fit in
(d) 4.2 g/L as the firmest allowed setting, with 8.4 g of air

questions.q:
900 g of water at room temperature (about 900 mL) is poured into a plastic box and frozen. The ice formed has a volume of 980 cm³ (an illustrative value).
(a) What is the mass of the ice? Explain.
(b) Find the density of the ice, to two decimal places.
(c) Find its relative density with respect to water, and say whether the ice will float.
(d) By what percentage did the volume increase on freezing?
(e) If the box had been a full glass bottle with its cap screwed tight, predict what might happen, and explain using (d).
questions.a: (a) 900 g: freezing does not change the mass, only the arrangement of particles. (b) 900 ÷ 980 = 0.92 g/cm³. (c) 0.92 ÷ 1 = 0.92 (no unit); it is less than 1, so the ice floats on water. (d) The volume rose by 980 − 900 = 80 cm³; 80 ÷ 900 × 100 = about 8.9%. (e) The bottle might crack: the water expands by about 9% as it turns to ice, but a full, tightly capped bottle has no room for the larger volume.
s: (a) 900 g, mass unchanged
(b) 0.92 g/cm³
(c) 0.92, floats
(d) about 8.9%
(e) bottle may crack because the ice needs about 9% more space

questions.q:
(a) The nozzle of a syringe completely full of water is sealed. Pushing the plunger very hard barely moves it. What does this show about water?
(b) Deep in the sea the pressure is very large. Using (a), predict whether sea water there is much denser than at the surface, if the temperature is the same.
questions.a: (a) Water is nearly incompressible: pressure can push its particles only very slightly closer, so its volume, and hence its density, hardly changes. (b) No: it is only slightly denser, because pressure has only a small effect on the density of a liquid.
s: (a) water is nearly incompressible
(b) only slightly denser, since pressure has a small effect on liquids

questions.q: The water in a pond cools slowly from 10 °C to 2 °C over a week, without freezing. At which temperature in this range will 1 kg of the pond water occupy the least volume?
